narrationScript: Now, let's explore another powerful way programs can receive input: **command-line arguments**. When you launch a program from your terminal, you can provide additional pieces of information right alongside the program's name. For instance, when you compile a C program, you might type `gcc -o myprogram myprogram.c`. Here, `-o` and `myprogram.c` are arguments passed to the `gcc` compiler. Your own C programs can easily access these arguments through special parameters in the `main` function. These are `int argc` and `char *argv[]`. `argc`, short for 'argument count', is an integer that tells you exactly how many arguments were provided on the command line, including the program's own name. So, if you run `./myprogram hello world`, `argc` would be 3. `argv`, or 'argument vector', is an array of strings. Each element in this array, `argv[i]`, is a string representing one of the command-line arguments. Importantly, `argv[0]` is always the name of your program itself. `argv[1]` is the first argument you typed, `argv[2]` the second, and so on, up to `argv[argc - 1]`. Command-line arguments are incredibly useful for making your programs more flexible and configurable, especially for tools that run in automated scripts. Remember, all arguments in `argv` are initially strings, so if you expect a number, you'll need to convert it using functions like `atoi()` for integers or the safer `strtol()` for more robust error handling.
deliveryNotes: Clearly explain the role of `argc` and `argv`
Highlight the importance of string-to-number conversion
